title: Pure (Sn 4.4)
hookLine: read it: purity isn't found by views or rites
tomorrow: someone calls their view the best. what does it cost them?
last: MEET THE FEAR · LOVE NOW · THIS LIFE, NOW.

lines: A CLEANSE. A DETOX. A FRESH NOTEBOOK.
PURITY YOU CAN SIGN UP FOR.
cards: A juice cleanse. A detox weekend. A fresh notebook on the first of the month.
A new morning routine that will finally fix everything. Purity is easy to sell, because it sounds like something you can sign up for, or get right.
The fourth poem in the chapter of eights takes that hope seriously, and then it brings in a monkey.

teach.h: I SEE THE PURE, THEY SAY.
teach.b: In paraphrase from the Sutta Nipata: some say, I see the pure, the highest, the healthy; seeing it is what makes a person pure. The poem pushes back.
If seeing the right view made someone pure, purity would come from something outside them, while they were still grasping.

teach.h: NOT FROM ANOTHER, NOT FROM RITES.
teach.b: The true brahmin, the poem's word for a really pure one, doesn't say purity comes from another: not from what's seen or heard, and not from rules and rites. Then the picture.
People let go of one thing and grab the next, like a monkey letting go of one branch only to seize another. The poem doesn't throw rules away.
It says leaning on them as the thing that makes you pure is one more branch. So the week's thread ties off here. Fear, wanting, the cave, the praised view: each one is a grip.
Purity, in this poem, isn't a better thing to grab. It's the hand opening.

how: Buddhists keep precepts and take part in rites such as chanting and offerings; teachers who read the chapter of eights use poems like this one to warn against treating those practices, or holding correct views, as what makes a person pure.

o: clean of grabbing, not made clean by a view
free of every mistake you've ever made
born into a family that keeps the old rites

games.q: the week's pictures — tap the pairs.
p: four roots that can be seen
glad if gotten, an arrow if lost
lets go of one branch to grab the next

s: the poem says rules and rites are what make a person pure
the true brahmin doesn't say purity comes from rules and rites, or from any view.
the poem pictures people grabbing views like a monkey grabbing branches
letting go of one only to seize the next.
the poem tells Buddhists to throw out every rule
it warns against leaning on rules as what makes you pure; it doesn't call them worthless.

games.q: your friend jumps from one wellness routine to the next, each one 'finally the one that fixes me.' by the poem, what's going on?
o: a monkey and branches: grabbing the next thing to be made pure.
she just hasn't found the right routine for her body yet.
routines are the problem; she should drop every one of them.
games.why: the poem doesn't fault the routines. it points at the grab: hoping the next branch will make you pure, and letting go only to seize another.

practice: Stand and walk slowly across the room and back, as many times as the bell allows.
Each time your mind grabs a branch, a plan, a worry, the next thing to check, notice the grab, let the hand of your attention open, and come back to the feel of your feet on the floor.

wordCard.voice: Pure: in this poem, not something you get by holding the right view or doing the right rite, but the letting go of grabbing.

orig.note: Pali: purity, cleanness. The poem is the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta, the eight verses on purity.

carryVoice: The line for today: not by views; the monkey can rest on one branch. A week of poems and endings, done.
